newsitem.title: JAPAN: Chirac says France must triple Asia market share.
newsitem.headline: Chirac says France must triple Asia market share.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, at the start of his first official visit to Japan, called on Sunday on French business to triple market share in Japan and the rest of Asia.
"We must go where growth is," Chirac told French businessmen at a reception at the French embassy in Tokyo. "We must triple our market share in Asia and equally in Japan," he said.
About 2,000 French businessmen and residents packed the green lawn and balcony of the embassy to hear Chirac.
"There are some who believe Japan is a closed market with insurmountable barriers to trade and impenetrable culture," Chirac said. "That is false. You are testimony to that."
French exports to Japan in 1995 totalled 28 billion francs ($5.5 billion), well behind Japan's main trading partner the United States.

Standing under France's tricolour and the European Community flag, Chirac announced that France's CNES (Centre National d'Etude Spatiales) and Japan's NASDA (National Space Development Agency) would sign a comprehensive cooperation plan on Monday.
"Japan is trying to become the world's second power in space," he said.
The plan includes possible development of equipment for use in international space stations, joint exploration of the solar system and joint observatory satellite development.
Chirac arrived in Tokyo early on Sunday amid tight security for a six-day visit to boost economic ties and restore relations damaged by French nuclear tests in the South Pacific last year.
Economic talks are expected to focus on French demands that Japan open its insurance, construction, aircraft and car manufacturing industries to French companies.
In case of nuclear protests, police were on duty on roads around the luxurious Hotel Okura where Chirac is staying.

Only a handful of anti-nuclear protesters turned up at the French embassy, holding posters of Chirac headlined "nuclear proliferation". The six demonstrators, including activist Ichiro Murakami, were hustled away by police as they unfolded a banner which declared in Japanese "Tahiti is crying".
Murakami staged a four-month sit-down protest in front of the French embassy in Tokyo during the French nuclear testing programme which ended in January.
Chirac is to spend four days in Tokyo as a state guest before making a private visit to Fukuoka, southwestern Japan, where he plans to see a sumo wrestling tournament.
In a Japanese newspaper interview on the eve of his arrival, Chirac said France wanted Tokyo to play a more active role in international affairs.
"In a period of world crisis, France looks to Japan as an important player to consult with," Chirac told the Asahi Shimbun newspaper.
